title: Five Things You Ask For --- Soap, Towel, Glass, Spoon, Plate

lessons.title: el jabón — a word that went abroad and came home
lessons.gloss: soap — Latin sapo, which Latin had itself borrowed from its northern neighbours

segments.text: Before a new run: how many times did English borrow febris? (Twice.) And what does dolere mean? (To hurt.)
el agua — what you use this with.
por favor — what you put on the end when you ask.
ja-BON, stress on the second syllable, which the written accent marks. The j is the jota again, the rasp at the back. see reference.
el jabón — "soap."
Latin sapo, saponem — and Latin did not make this word. It borrowed it from the Germanic peoples on its northern frontier, who used the stuff on their hair before anybody in Rome used it for washing.

So English soap and jabón are one word, and the English one is the one that stayed at home. Spanish has it back after a long detour: Germanic into Latin, Latin into Spanish. Saponify and saponification are the late loans, taken straight from the Latin form.
Words move with things. Rome had better roads and better law; the north had better soap. Trade decides vocabulary far more often than conquest does.
Not every Latin word is Roman.
Latin was borrowing from its neighbours the whole time, and a word can be perfectly good Latin and still be an import. Jabón has been abroad and come back, and nothing in the sound of it says so.

segments.instruction: jabón and soap, and hear one word twice
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *jabón* and *soap*, and hear one word twice]

segments.text: Where did Latin get sapo? (From its Germanic neighbours.) Is English soap borrowed from Spanish? (No — it never left; it is the same word at home.)

lessons.title: la toalla — the Germanic layer, still in the bathroom
lessons.gloss: a towel — a Frankish word that went into French and came out in two languages

segments.text: Before the new one: where did Latin get sapo? (From its Germanic neighbours.)
el jabón — what you use before you need this.
el agua — and what you are drying off.
to-A-lla, stress on the a. The ll is a y sound for most speakers, and something closer to a j in the River Plate. see reference.
la toalla — "a towel."
Another Germanic word, and this time both languages took it. Frankish thwahlja, a cloth for washing, became Old French toaille, and out of that Spanish has toalla and English has towel.

Two words in a row now that are not Latin at the bottom. Spanish is a Latin language with a Germanic layer laid over the top, and that layer sits mostly in the house and the wardrobe — the words the settlers brought along with the things themselves.
The -alla ending is the giveaway. A Latin word would not have arrived in that shape; a French one would. Spanish borrowed this from its neighbour, not from its parent.
Two Germanic words, side by side, in the plainest room of the house.
That is not an accident. The most domestic vocabulary in a Romance language is often the least Roman, because that is where the incomers actually lived.
Is toalla a Latin word? (No — Frankish, through French.) Which English word is the same one? (Towel.)

lessons.title: el vaso — named for the job, not the material
lessons.gloss: a glass — Latin vas, a vessel: named for what it does, not for what it is made of

segments.text: Before the new one: is toalla a Latin word? (No — Frankish, through French.)
el agua — what goes in it.
la toalla — the thing before this one.
VA-so, stress on the first syllable. The v is the same soft sound as b — the letters differ and the sound does not. see reference.
el vaso — "a glass," the thing you drink out of.

Latin vas, vasis: a vessel, a container of any sort. Spanish names the object by what it does rather than by what it is made of, which is why a plastic one is still a vaso and an English glass made of plastic is a small embarrassment.

English has three of them at three different weights. A vase holds flowers. A vessel holds wine, or cargo, or blood. The vascular system is the body's plumbing, named by anatomists reaching for the same Latin.
And notice the letter. Vaso begins with the sound you have been giving to b. Spanish writes v and says something very close to b, and that was true long before the spelling settled down.
Three things you can ask for, and three different sources.
Germanic, Frankish, Latin. A tray of ordinary objects in a Spanish kitchen is a small map of who passed through.

segments.instruction: un vaso de agua, por favor
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *un vaso de agua, por favor*]

segments.instruction: vaso and vase, and hear the container in both
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *vaso* and *vase*, and hear the container in both]

segments.text: What did vas mean in Latin? (A vessel or container.) Why is a plastic one still a vaso? (Because the word names the job, not the material.)

lessons.title: la cuchara — a snail shell with a handle
lessons.gloss: a spoon — Latin cochlear, from cochlea, a snail shell you dug the snail out with

segments.text: Before the new one: what did vas mean in Latin? (A vessel.)
el vaso — the thing before this one.
la comida — what you need this for.
cu-CHA-ra, stress in the middle. The ch is one sound, as in English church, and never a k. see reference.
la cuchara — "a spoon."
Latin cochlear, a spoon, from cochlea, a snail shell. The Romans ate snails and used the shell to get them out, and the tool kept the name of the shell long after it had stopped being one.

Cochlea is still in English, unchanged, for the spiral inside your ear — named by an anatomist who thought it looked like the shell. So the spoon and the inner ear are the same Latin snail, arriving a thousand years apart by two completely different routes.
A tool named after the thing it replaced is one of the commonest patterns in any vocabulary. The name outlives the object, and nobody notices until somebody pulls the word open.
Four things, and each one is a small piece of history you can hold.
Soap from the north, a towel from the Franks, a vessel from Rome, and a snail shell with a handle on it.

segments.instruction: cochlea and cuchara, the shell and the spoon
segments.source: [YOU SAY: *cochlea* and *cuchara*, the shell and the spoon]

segments.text: What is a cochlea? (A snail shell.) What else in English carries the name? (The spiral of the inner ear.)

lessons.title: el plato — flat, in Greek, before anything else
lessons.gloss: a plate — Greek platys, flat: the same flatness in a plaza and in a platypus

segments.text: Before the last of the five: what is a cochlea? (A snail shell.) And what did vas mean? (A vessel.)
la cuchara — what you put beside it.
por favor — what closes every one of these requests.
PLA-to, stress on the first syllable. The l stays clear and forward, and the pl is said cleanly with no vowel slipped in. see reference.
el plato — "a plate."
Not Latin at the bottom: Greek platys, flat or broad. Latin took it in as plattus, and out of that Spanish has plato and English has plate.

The same Greek flatness turns up all over. A plaza is a flat open space — Latin platea, a broad street. A plateau is a flat high place. A platypus is a flat-foot. And English flat itself is the Germanic cousin of platys, from the same ancient root by the other road.
Five things you can now ask for. The asking itself you have had for a long while: por favor on the end of any of them, and the sentence is finished.
Five: el jabón, la toalla, el vaso, la cuchara, el plato.
Germanic, Frankish, Latin, Latin, Greek. Five ordinary objects and five different origins — which is the honest answer to the question of where Spanish words come from.

segments.instruction: all five in order — el jabón, la toalla, el vaso, la cuchara, el plato
segments.source: [YOU SAY: all five in order — *el jabón*, *la toalla*, *el vaso*, *la cuchara*, *el plato*]

segments.text: What does platys mean? (Flat.) What is a platypus, taken apart? (A flat-foot.) And where did Latin get sapo? (From its Germanic neighbours.)
